items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now les
items.summary:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

items.title: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:
items.summary:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

items.summary:
𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰'𝘀 𝗙𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝟱.𝟭 𝘃𝘀 𝗠𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘀 𝟱.𝟭: 𝟰 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀

[Follow for more such AI Educational content]

Anthropic's reported safety findings highlight a critical shift: more capable AI agents need smarter safeguards, not just stricter restrictions.

Here's what matters.

𝟭. 𝗔𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀
• Less unauthorized behavior outside test environments.
• Reduced motivated reasoning and reward hacking.
• Critical for agents executing autonomous tasks.
𝟮. 𝗙𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗙𝗮𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀
• 85% fewer biology safeguard triggers on tested benign queries.
• ~60% fewer cyber interventions per tested session.
• Better safety precision means fewer legitimate tasks blocked.
𝟯. 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗰𝘆
• Zero-data-retention arrangements.
• Customer-controlled cloud storage and human review.
• Safeguards designed for regulated environments.
𝟰. 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘃𝘀 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀
• Fable 5.1: Public access with stronger restrictions.
• Mythos 5.1: Gated access for vetted organizations.
• Same underlying capabilities, different safeguard policies.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻
Agent safety isn't just about blocking harmful prompts.
It's about preventing unauthorized actions, minimizing false positives, protecting enterprise data, and maintaining human control.
𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲.

𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜'𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸: 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀, 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀, 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 & 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁

OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra launch has intensified the AGI debate.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang declared, "AGI has arrived," while OpenAI President Greg Brockman described the beginning of the AGI era.

But beyond those claims, something more practical is happening.

𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸.

Here's how the ecosystem fits together.

𝗔. 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀

• GPT-6 Astra: Flagship model for complex reasoning, coding, computer use, cybersecurity, and science.

• Benchmark scores: 98% on FrontierMath Tier 4, 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3, and 100% on ExploitBench.

• GPT-6.1 Sol: Near-Astra capabilities at a lower API cost.

• GPT-6 Sol and Luna: Models optimized for different capability, speed, and cost requirements.

𝗕. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 & 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀

• Agents SDK: Build and orchestrate AI agents using Python or TypeScript.

• Responses API: Combine reasoning, tool calls, and multistep workflows.

• MCP: Connect agents to external tools and enterprise systems.

𝗖. 𝗔𝗜 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘀 & 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲

• Codex: Handles software engineering tasks, from writing code to testing.

• ChatGPT Agent: Performs research and multistep tasks using browsers and connected tools.

• ChatGPT Work: Executes workflows across business applications, documents, and data.

• ChatGPT Images: Generates and edits visual content.

𝗗. 𝗩𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲 & 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗔𝗜

• GPT-Live: Supports natural, full-duplex voice conversations.

• Realtime API: Enables low-latency voice agents and interactive applications.

𝗘. 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 & 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲

• Persistent memory: Retains useful context across conversations.

• Preparedness Framework: Evaluates frontier AI risks, including cybersecurity capabilities.

• Safety monitoring: Detects risky behavior and unauthorized actions.

Notably, Astra became OpenAI's first model to reach the Critical cybersecurity capability threshold.

𝗙. 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 & 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴

• API model: gpt-6-astra

• Availability: OpenAI API, Microsoft Azure, and AWS Bedrock.

• Standard API pricing: $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.

• Context window: 1.05 million tokens.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘀?

The value of AI is moving beyond generating responses.

It's increasingly about agents that can research, write code, operate applications, access enterprise knowledge, and complete workflows.

But greater autonomy also requires stronger access controls, monitoring, and human oversight.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗸𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆

The important question is no longer just "Which AI model should we use?"

It's also "Which tasks can we safely delegate to AI?"

That's the shift enterprise AI leaders need to prepare for.

"Building good multi-agent AI systems is just as hard as building good human teams: they both face the same information processing tradeoff between alignment and differentiation. It won't magically work better with AI," he said. [...] Other early research suggests another failing across AI teams that doesn't relate to ethical boundaries being crossed: failure to recognize who the real expert is.

Unlike human teams, AI teams "consistently fail to match their expert agent's performance, even when explicitly told who the expert is," according to a study conducted by Emory University and Stanford University researchers. items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary:
Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which specializes in logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the new methods earlier this year to analyze parcel sorting data and test updates to robot behavior. Tests showed an increased capacity of over 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot; the change is now deployed across 30% of the company’s U.S. fleet. [...] Ken Goldberg

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are controlled,” Goldberg said. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

items.title: Autonomous EV developer Humble Robotics adds $51M to expand - TT
items.summary:
Humble Robotics raised $51 million in Series A financing, bringing its total funding to $75 million less than a year after its founding.
 The company is developing the Humble Hauler, a battery-electric, cabless Class 8 autonomous vehicle for regional freight routes under 250 miles.
 Humble will fund customer pilots, testing, early manufacturing and expansion into vehicles for 40-foot containers and 53-foot dry van and refrigerated trailers. [...] Stay on top of transportation news: [Get TTNews in your inbox.]

Humble Robotics secured $51 million in new financing, bringing the autonomous electric vehicle developer’s total funding to $75 million less than a year after its founding. [...] The Hauler uses vision-language-action models and is equipped with cameras, lidar and radar that provide 360-degree coverage of its surroundings. The battery-electric skateboard platform has an aerodynamic shield at the front, while shipping containers can be attached through a twist-lock interface.

items.title: FDA seeks input on telesurgery, autonomous robotics
items.summary: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning and connectivity are driving expansion of robotic applications in a wide range of clinical settings, the FDA said. Increases in processing power, data storage and computational efficiency are enabling progress in robotic systems with autonomous capabilities. [...] In another example of teleoperation, manufacturers are developing devices that enable technicians to remotely perform ultrasounds, the FDA said. Robotic devices include stereotactic navigation systems, imaging devices and endoluminal navigation devices. [...] The FDA is asking the robotics community to submit comments on the discussion paper by Jan. 5. Ahead of that deadline, a public workshop to discuss the topics raised in the paper is scheduled for Dec. 2-3.

items.title: NVIDIA launches GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL - The Robot Report
items.summary:
Walden Robotics is using Isaac Sim’s photorealistic rendering to train and evaluate its general-purpose robot in virtual environments for manufacturing and logistics. Dexmate is exploring how coding agents can rehearse and refine manipulation strategies in Isaac Sim before executing them on its Vega robot. [...] Robotics developers are already putting NVIDIA’s latest technology to the test. A number of developers are using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton. At CoRL, Skild AI announced Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning, or STEEL, a new rigid-body physics solver built on Newton to accelerate robot training with Isaac Lab. [...] Nexuni is testing GR00T 2 for robotic laundry. Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing, and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases.

MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained.

items.title: Kenwood High School JROTC Robotics Program earns regional recognition - ClarksvilleNow.com
items.summary:
“I am proud of the national-level success of Kenwood’s Robotics Team. It reflects the faculty, JROTC instructors, and cadets’ hard work and dedication toward creating an elite mindset at the school,” Lightner said.

Dr Nigel Anderson, Kenwood High School Principal, noted “The robotics program complements the leadership development and citizenship training provided through JROTC while exposing students to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines.” [...] CLARKSVILLE TN – The Kenwood High School JROTC Robotics Program has grown from a single robotics team into a four-team program that is competing successfully at regional and national-level events. The program currently fields Teams 26163X, 26163A, 26163L, and 26163S, providing students with opportunities to develop skills in engineering, programming, and problem-solving. [...] During the current robotics’ competition season, Team 26163X captured first place at the Tennessee State Fair Robotics Competition. The team followed that performance with another first-place finish at a competition in Elizabethton, Tennessee, where it also received a technical award recognizing excellence in robot design and engineering.
